segments.text:
These lines continue the function `render` that starts at line 341. They write the heading and the first paragraph of section 1.5.
- `a1p` is the list of the processes of baseline A-1, read from `threads120.csv` of the run of 2026-11-13.
- `a1first` is the launch time of its first process.
- The three check numbers in that paragraph are the places of the checks `sha-bw`, `A-args` and `A-order` in the list `D['checks']`, counted from 1 as in section 1.4.
segments.heading: Section 1.5: differences between the 2026-11-13 procedure and part A

segments.text:
Point 1, the one-thread phase (the part of the 2026-11-13 run with one thread per process, before the 120-thread part).
- Line 940 adds the first and the last launch time of that phase to the set `OTHER_DAY`. These two times are text from the csv. The function `hmd` (line 72), which adds a time of another day to this set, does not format them.
- The guard in line 941 checks that the folder name of A-1 holds the date 2026-11-13. The template states that date as fixed text.
- The sentence prints the number of one-thread processes. build_facts.py counted the `-- binary` header lines of `one-thread.csv` for it.
- It also prints `a1first` and the 1-minute load average from the header line of that process.

Points 2 to 4.
- Point 2 prints the start state of the three part A sessions from `evd`, which holds the steps of the run by folder tag.
- Point 3 prints `ra_limit` and `ra_sleep`. Line 737 took both numbers from the text of ra.sh: the highest count of runnable tasks at which the wait ends, and the sleep after the wait in seconds.
- The second sentence of point 3 says that the script of 2026-11-13 built the binaries, ran a self-test and the one-thread phase, and had no wait. It is fixed text. No guard in this file checks it. The local copy of that script (run_kernels.sh) agrees with it. It runs the build, the self-test, the one-thread phase and the 120-thread part in this order, and it holds no `sleep` command and no wait loop.
- Point 4 is fixed text.

Builds two sentences about hardware error records during the baselines A-2 and A-3. Point 8 prints them.
- `a2r` holds the records of the saved journal with a time between the first launch of `A1.csv` and the first launch of `A2.csv`. build_facts.py gave each record the last process of `A1.csv` that was launched at or before it.
- The loop groups the records by their second. A guard checks that all records of one second belong to one process. Each group becomes one text piece with the count, the time, the process and the journal lines.
- `a2txt` gives the number of records and their severity, or the words `0 records` when `a2r` is empty.
- `a3txt` gives the number of records in the time span of the three processes of A-3.

Points 5 to 7.
- Point 5 prints the start of the boot of the 2026-11-13 run. build_facts.py took it from the first line of the saved journal.
- The time from that start to `a1first` is divided by 86400 s and printed in days with 1 decimal.
- For the rerun, `dur` formats the time from the first Linux kernel log line of its boot to the start of go.sh.
- Points 6 and 7 are fixed text.

Point 8, hardware error records.
- It prints the time and the line number of the first record in the journal of the 2026-11-09 boot. The words "during the one-thread phase of that run" are fixed text. No guard compares the time of that record with the times of the phase.
- `records_in_120` is the number of journal lines with the tag `[Hardware Error]` between the end of the one-thread phase and the end of the 120-thread part of A-1. build_facts.py counts lines for this value. For A-2 and A-3 it counts records, and one record has more than one line. The value is 0 in the facts sheet [Ref4].
- The sentences `a2txt` and `a3txt` follow.
- The statement for the rerun is fixed text: the Linux kernel log was not read, and the count is marked as "Insufficient data".

Point 9, the module count of the 2026-11-13 run. It prints the boot start, the number from the journal line `This system has N DIMM sockets`, and the date text of the last line of the saved Linux kernel log. The guard in line 997 checks that the probe.txt of that run holds neither the text `MemTotal` nor the text `boot_id`, as the first sentence states.

Point 10, the memory speed of the baseline boot.
- `qt` is the file time of the saved settings list `questions.json`, read as UTC. A settings list is a file of the settings tool with one entry per firmware setting.
- `inboot(t)` returns the number of the last boot in the boot history of the DIMM report that started at or before the time `t`.
- The guard checks that `qt` and `a1first` lie in the same boot.
- The sentence prints `qt`, the value of the setting "DIMM Frequency" in that list, and the speed and its end time from the DIMM report.

Point 11, the second baseline A-2.
- `a2opts` collects the option texts `--cpus ...` and `--per-thread` of every A-2 process. A guard checks that all processes used one option set and that no process ran a copy kernel.
- `ap` describes the run folder that ended shortly before A-2. `a2gap` is the time from its end to the first launch of `A1.csv`, in seconds.
- The guard in lines 1012 to 1016 tests the patterns that point 11 states about that folder. Every process in its two csv files (A5.csv and A6.csv) ran `bw_new` with 1 thread. Its launches.txt holds as many entries as these two files hold processes, and it names the same two files. Its times are in order. `a2gap` is above 0 s and below 60 s. The header line of the first process of `A1.csv` is line 1 of that file. The step list in line 1 of the env.txt of the run folder `ap` ends with A5 and A6.
- That step list holds three steps. The first one is A7. The guard does not test A7. The folder holds four text files of A7 and no csv file of A7.
- `extra['a2pre_txt']` keeps the text about this gap. facts_text4.py uses it again.

Point 12, four settings of Linux that were compared between the two boots.
- `cmd72` is the Linux kernel command line of the rerun from the go.sh log. `rel72` is the release text after `vmlinuz-` in it.
- `thp80` is the huge page setting in env.txt of the A-2 run.
- Five guards check: the settings were saved inside the boot of the 8000 MT/s baselines. The Linux kernel release is equal. The command line is equal. gov.txt holds the governor name and the frequency value of the go.sh log. The huge page setting is equal.
- Then the point is written with one sub-bullet per setting. Each sub-bullet names the files and the lines that hold the two values.

Point 13, firmware settings: the data and seven guards.
- `fb`, `fx` and `fr` are the three saved settings lists: from the baseline boot, after the first change of a setting, and after the set-back. The set-back is the step that set the two changed settings to their earlier values again.
- `sx1`, `sx2`, `srv` and `sdm` are the four reply files `set.txt`. A reply file holds what the settings tool answered to a change. `fin` is the last reading of the memory speed.
- `one_set` returns the one reply of a file. Its guard checks that the file holds exactly one reply to a change and that this reply says `modified: true`.
- The guards check: the list after the set-back holds the same entries as the baseline list. "TXREQ Min" and "TXREQ Max" were changed and then set back to the baseline values. The dates and file times of the records are in the stated order. The list after the first change differs in "TXREQ Min" only. The DIMM report holds three text pieces that the text uses.
- The guard in line 1081 is about "DIMM Frequency". The reply to the change and the last reading both hold the speed of try6.txt (7200 MT/s). The baseline list holds the speed that point 10 prints (8000 MT/s). Point 10 reads its value from the same file as the baseline list. So this part of the guard compares two readings of one file. The guard holds neither of the two numbers as a fixed value.

Writes point 13 with its first four sub-bullets: the settings list of the baseline boot with its counts of readable and unreadable values, the two changes for another test, the set-back with the values read back, and the list after the set-back. Every number, date and line number comes from `fw`. The setting names in the first and the third sub-bullet are fixed text. The count of the values that were not compared is `unavailable + store_error` of the list after the set-back.

Writes the last three sub-bullets of point 13: the change of the memory speed with its last reading, the result of the search for reply files and settings lists under `R`, and the limits.
- The guard in line 1122 checks that the list after the first change holds as many entries with the text "ValueUnavailable" as the baseline list.
- The "Insufficient data" sentence about the firmware settings of the boot of the rerun is fixed text. Only the first 8 characters of the boot id are placed in it.
- `extra['fw']` keeps three values for facts_text4.py. That file reads two of them: `set_back` and `readable` [Ref3].

**Range of the old read kernel at 8000 MT/s**, for the text that rule F1 point 5 requires.
- `a12o` selects the records of `bw_old read` in the data sets A-1 and A-2. The data set A-3 also holds `bw_old read` records. This line leaves them out. The comparison of part A in line 425 uses all three data sets (`A80o`, line 420).
- The guard checks that they come from 4 processes: the first process of each file in round 1, and the last process of each file in round 2.
- `rng(a12o)` takes the lowest and the highest `GBps` of all these intervals together. `sp` prints both ends with 2 decimals, and `nn` prints the counts. The sentence prints no median and no mean.
- In the facts sheet the result is 464.42 to 467.06 GB/s from 12 intervals of 4 processes. With the 9 intervals of the 3 processes of A-3 the range is 463.58 to 469.03 GB/s [Ref4] [Ref6].

Two guards and one bullet for the words "after one-thread work and directly after 120-thread work" of the sentence before.
- The first guard checks that in round 2 the process before `bw_old read` in the file is `bw_new read`.
- `lgap` returns the seconds between the launches of the last two processes of a file. The second guard checks that this time is above 0 s and below 10 s in A-1 and in A-2.
- The bullet prints both times.
Writes the heading of section 2 and its first lines. All of this is fixed text.
segments.heading: Section 2: the decisions (a) to (r)

segments.text:
`dec` holds the eight decisions (a) to (h), made before or during the run. The sentences are fixed text. The loop writes one bullet per decision with its letter. The placed values are:
- reference numbers, and the number of the check `sha-bw`,
- `secA`, the interval length of part A,
- the launch time of F72d12 in hours and minutes,
- for decision (h): the file times of the rules file and of `local.sha`, the seconds between them, the start of go.sh, and `rules_lead`. `rules_lead` is the time from the time written in the rules file to the start of go.sh, in seconds (line 381).

Counts for decision (p).
- `bwxp` maps each process of the four data sets of the first runner bwx (`BWX`) to its field `start`, the value of the runner option `--start`.
- In the source of the runner bwx (bwx.c), `--start common` makes every thread start at byte 0 of its buffer. `--start offset` makes thread i start at byte (i x 37 mod n) x 2 MiB of its buffer. n is the number of 2 MiB blocks of the buffer.
- `bwx_off` is the number of processes with the value `offset`.
- The guard checks that both values `common` and `offset` occur and that no other value occurs.
- In the facts sheet these are 24 processes, 12 of them with `offset` [Ref4].

`dec2` holds the ten decisions (i) to (r), made after the numbers were seen. The first two state the method of the rate and of the ratio. Both are fixed text: no line derives them from the code.
- **(i) Rate per interval.** Part A: the column `aggregate_GBps` of the csv. bwx runners: the bytes of each thread divided by the elapsed time of that thread, added over the threads. build_facts.py and facts_data.py set the field `GBps` in this way [Ref1] [Ref2]. build_facts.py rounds the rates to 0.001 GB/s only when it writes facts.json.
- **(j) Ratio new/old in part A.** The median of the 3 `bw_new` intervals divided by the median of the 3 `bw_old` intervals of the same session and round. Line 298 computes it.
- Line 299 computes the lowest and the highest ratio of single intervals as (j) states: lowest `bw_new` / highest `bw_old`, and highest `bw_new` / lowest `bw_old`.

Decisions (k) to (q). All are fixed text, except the counts in (p).
- (k) names the 8000 MT/s side of the overlap test for parts L and C: the pool of the data sets L-1 to L-4. Line 417 builds this pool.
- (l) says that only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 of the earlier bwx12 and bwx11 rows are used. build_facts.py applies this filter when it builds the records of L-2 to L-4, R0 and R0b [Ref1]. For L-1, `pool` applies it through its position argument (line 417).
- (m) says that row X2d12 is shown and not used.
- (n), (o) and (q) name three views that were added after the numbers were seen.
- (p) places `len(bwxp)`, the number and the names of the `BWX` data sets, `bwx_off`, and the number of processes with `--start common`.

Decision (r) and the loop that writes the list.
- (r) is fixed text with one reference number. It says that the rules contradict each other about a comparison of part C with 8000 MT/s. It says that this sheet gives a wording for two rows of part C: oldread, and asmread directly after oldread.
- The guard in line 1242 checks that `dec2` has 10 entries, one per letter from i to r.
- The loop writes one bullet per decision with its letter.

Writes the headings of section 3 and of section 3.1. `secA` is the interval length of part A as text (`0.5 s` in the facts sheet [Ref4]). The loop writes one bullet per session with its folder tag and its start state. The last sentence says how to read the table that follows.
segments.heading: Section 3.1: part A, old against new

segments.text:
**Table 1 of section 3.1: one row per process.**
- `slabel` maps a session number to its start state text.
- The outer loop runs once for each of the 6 pairs of `N['pa']`. There is one pair per session and round.
- The inner loop takes the four processes of a pair: `bw_old read`, `bw_new read`, `bw_old asmread` and `bw_new asmread`. This is the order of the table rows. In round 1 it is also the order of the launches. In round 2 the four processes were launched in the reverse order (column Launch) [Ref4].
- `cell` is the list of the 3 interval records of that process, sorted by interval number (lines 292 to 294).
- The processes of write, copy, asmwrite and asmcopy are not in this table. Section 5 of the facts sheet gives the lowest, the median and the highest rate of their intervals for each kernel, binary and session [Ref4].

The cells of one row. No rate is added to another rate here.
- Launch: characters 12 to 19 of `launch_utc`, the time as `HH:MM:SS`. Load at launch: 2 decimals.
- Interval 1, 2, 3: the records with the interval numbers 0, 1 and 2. Each cell shows `g(r['GBps'])` and, in brackets, the pass count. `GBps` is column 7 (`aggregate_GBps`) of one interval row of `threads120.csv`. Line 2 of that file gives its formula: the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread [Ref7].
- Median: `med(cell)`, the middle value of the 3 rates, printed with 2 decimals.
- Slowest to fastest thread: the lowest `per_thread_min_GBps` and the highest `per_thread_max_GBps` of the 3 intervals. These are columns 8 and 9 of the interval rows.
- Source: the reference number of the csv, and the line numbers of the first and the third interval row. `r0['folder'][2:]` removes the leading `R/` of the folder text.
- Example, session 1, round 1, `bw_old read`: 467.83 GB/s (954 passes), 467.92 GB/s (951 passes), 465.38 GB/s (944 passes), median 467.83 GB/s, source lines 4-6 of the csv [Ref4].
`table` turns the column titles and the rows into Markdown lines. `L.extend` appends them to the sheet. The table has 24 rows: 6 pairs with 4 processes each.

**Table 2 of section 3.1: one row per pair.** `analyse` computed every value in lines 297 to 300 from the `GBps` values before rounding. These lines only format them.
- `old_med`, `new_med`: the medians of the 3 intervals of `bw_old read` and of `bw_new read`, printed by `g` with 2 decimals.
- Ratio new/old: `new_med / old_med`, printed with 3 decimals.
- New below old: the drop `(1 - ratio) x 100`, printed by `pc` with 1 decimal.
- `ratio_lo` to `ratio_hi`: lowest `bw_new` interval / highest `bw_old` interval, and highest `bw_new` interval / lowest `bw_old` interval.
- The last two columns: the median of `bw_old asmread` / `old_med`, and the median of `bw_new asmread` / `old_med`.
- Example, session 1, round 1: 467.83 and 330.59 GB/s, ratio 0.707, drop 29.3 % [Ref4].

The first three bullets under the tables.
- `passes_new` holds the pass counts of all `bw_new read` intervals of the 6 pairs, each value once, sorted. `passes_old` holds the pass counts of all `bw_old read` intervals.
- `top` is the pair with the highest `ratio_hi`. Bullet 1 prints the number of pairs, that ratio with its session and round, and the two rates that form it: the highest `bw_new` rate and the lowest `bw_old` rate of that pair.
- The words "below the old read kernel in all pairs" are fixed text. The guards in lines 396 and 397 check them before any line of the sheet is written.
- Bullet 2 is fixed text.
- Bullet 3 prints the lowest and the highest of the 12 values `ao_ratio` and `an_ratio` of the 6 pairs, with 3 decimals. Its second sentence ("So the lower rate belongs to the load-only loop, not to the binary") is fixed text. No guard checks it.

Bullets 4 and 5 under the tables.
- Bullet 4 prints the pass counts. For `bw_new read` it lists each value when there are 2 to 4 different values, and it prints the lowest and the highest value in every other case. For `bw_old read` it prints the lowest and the highest value.
- In the facts sheet these are "664, 718 or 719" and "919 to 968" passes per interval [Ref4].
- Bullet 5 is fixed text: the limit of part A by rule V3.

Writes the heading of section 3.2 and three fixed bullets. `secX` is the interval length of the bwx12 parts as text (`6 s` in the facts sheet [Ref4]).
- The first bullet says that asmread is the same loop as the new read kernel: 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B. This is fixed text. This script reads no machine code.
- The saved objdump listing of bwx12 agrees with that bullet. The tool objdump prints the machine code of a binary as assembler text. In `k_asmread` and in `k_read`, one loop pass holds 8 `ldp` instructions on `q` registers and moves the pointer by 256 bytes.
- The second bullet states the formula of the drop. Line 314 computes the drop with this formula.
- The words "oldread then asmread" of the heading are fixed text. No line of this file tests the position of these two kernels in part L, in control I or in F72d12. The records agree with the words: in each of these processes oldread is at position 0 and asmread is at position 1 of both rounds. In round 1, oldread runs directly after read_1pl, the last kernel of round 0 [Ref6].
segments.heading: Section 3.2: parts L and I, oldread against asmread

segments.text:
Builds one table row from one pair `p` of the function `pairs` (line 304). `o` is the oldread record and `a_` is the asmread record of the same process and round.
- Tag: the folder tag. For the data set F72d12 the fixed text `F72d12` is used. The tag of such a record is the name of its csv file without `.csv`, which is `a6456`.
- Rates: `g(o['GBps'])` and `g(a_['GBps'])`. Each is the sum of `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9` over the T rows of one interval (one row per thread), printed with 2 decimals.
- `m0 + m1`: the sums over the threads of mesh 0 and of mesh 1. Each value is rounded separately. So the two printed values can add up to 0.01 GB/s more or less than the printed rate.
- Drop: `pc(p['drop_asmread'])`. That is `(1 - asmread / oldread) x 100`, printed with 1 decimal.
- Source: the csv and the line numbers of the two I rows. The printed rate is not the value of the I row. The I row holds the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread. Example: line 128 of the csv of T72L1 holds 462.29 GB/s, and the table shows 462.30 GB/s [Ref8] [Ref4].
segments.heading: Function `lrow`: one table row of section 3.2

segments.text:
These lines belong to `render` again. They fill the table of section 3.2 with one row per pair. A process has two pairs: round 0 and round 1.
- `N['pl']` gives the rows of part L, `N['pi']` the rows of control I, and `N['pf']` the rows of the earlier run F72d12. In the facts sheet these are 6, 4 and 2 rows [Ref4].
- The label of a part L row holds the text of the constant `STANDIN` (line 30): asmread is used in place of the new read kernel.
- The table leaves out the intervals of read_nop96, read_nop256 and read_1pl of the same processes. Section 4.8 of the facts sheet gives the lowest and the highest rate of each of these three kernels for part L, for control I and for F72d12 [Ref4].

The four bullets under the table of section 3.2. They hold no rate.
- `gl` holds the gaps of the three part L steps in seconds, each value once. The words "after the last 120-thread process of part A of its session" are fixed text. No guard in this file checks which step ran before a part L step. The table of section 1.1 of the facts sheet agrees with the words: it lists the steps in the order of their first launch, and each part L step follows the part A step of its session [Ref4].
- The control I bullet prints the load at launch and the gap of the steps T72I1 and T72I2.
- The F72d12 bullet prints the seconds from the first Linux kernel log line of the boot to its launch, and the load at launch.
- `fenv` holds the values that facts_data.py read from env.txt of F72d12. The process list of that file is sorted by %CPU, highest first. The guard checks that it lists at least 2 processes, and that the %CPU of the first one is more than 10 times the highest %CPU in the env.txt files of the rerun.
- The last bullet prints these two processes with their %CPU and their line numbers.

Writes the heading of section 3.3 and four fixed bullets. They name the kernels and the two orders cfwd and crev. They state that each drop is computed against oldread of the same process and round.
- The first bullet says that `read` of bwx12 is the new read kernel and that `oldread` of bwx12 is the old read kernel. This is fixed text. This script reads no machine code.
- The saved objdump listings agree with that bullet. The listing of bwx12 (the file listing.txt of its build of 2026-11-15) holds its functions `k_read` and `k_oldread`. The file probe.txt in the folder of baseline A-1 (the run of 2026-11-13) holds `k_read` of bw_new and `k_read` of bw_old.
- Both files describe the binaries of the rerun. The record of that bwx12 build (build.txt) holds the sha256 of this listing.txt and the sha256 of bwx12 that the driver script go.sh tests. That probe.txt holds the sha256 values of bw_old and bw_new that ra.sh, the script of part A, tests.
- `k_read` of bwx12 and `k_read` of bw_new hold the same 13 instructions. `k_oldread` of bwx12 and `k_read` of bw_old hold the same 70 instructions. In these functions the two listings differ only in addresses and in the function name that a label shows.
- First kind of address difference: each function lies at another place in its binary. So the address of each line differs, and so does the printed target of each branch inside a function (1 branch in the new read kernel, 3 in the old one). The distance from the start of the function to the target is equal in both listings.
- Second kind: 3 instructions of the old read kernel name an address outside the function. They are two `adrp` instructions (each forms the address of a memory page) and one `bl` instruction (a function call). These addresses differ. The 3 instructions lie outside the loop.
segments.heading: Section 3.3: part C, oldread, read and asmread

segments.text:
**Table 1 of section 3.3: one row per process and round.** The loop runs once for each pair of `N['pc']`. Each pair holds the oldread, the read and the asmread record of one process and round.
- `x` is the entry of `X` with the same folder tag. It gives the order (`cfwd` or `crev`) and the path of the csv.
- `cellf` prints one rate with 2 decimals, its position in the sequence, and the kernel that ran directly before. `mm` prints the two mesh sums.
- The two drop columns print `drop_read` and `drop_asmread` with 1 decimal. Line 314 computed them as `(1 - GBps of the kernel / GBps of oldread) x 100`, with oldread of the same process and round.
- Source: the csv and the line numbers of the three I rows.
- In the facts sheet the table has 8 rows: 4 processes with 2 rounds each [Ref4].

**Table 2 of section 3.3: the groups.** `C` is a second name for `Crec`, the list of all part C records (line 400). `groups` holds six entries.
- The first five are the groups of `CG`, each with its records and its drops against oldread (lines 402 to 409).
- The sixth entry selects all oldread records of part C, and it has no drops.
- The third item of each entry, for example `cfwd, rounds 0 and 1`, is fixed text.

One table row per group. The read intervals after oldread and the read intervals after asmread stay in separate rows.
- `rng(rs)` takes the lowest and the highest `GBps` of the records of the group, and the counts.
- Folder tags: the tags of the records, each once, in the order of the records.
- n: `nn` with `boots=False` prints intervals / processes.
- Min to max: `sp` prints the lowest and the highest rate with 2 decimals.
- Last column: the lowest and the highest drop of the group with 1 decimal, or `-` for the oldread row.
- The bullet after the table is fixed text: the limit of rule V2 point 5. The process names T72C2 and T72C4 and the number 2 in it are fixed text too. No guard compares them with the records. The table of section 1.1 agrees with them: it lists T72C2 as part C (crev) of session 2 and T72C4 as part C (crev) after the steps of session 3, and the other two part C steps as cfwd [Ref4].

Writes the heading of section 3.4 and prepares its table.
- `gL`, `gI`, `gC` and `gA` are the results of `rng` for asmread of part L, asmread of control I, `read` of part C and `bw_new read` of part A. Only counts of these results are used below: `n`, `procs` and `sessions` of `gL` and of `gA`, and `n` and `procs` of `gI`. No later line reads `gC`.
- `tags` returns the folder tags of a record list, each once.
- `cpair(key, what)` returns the table entry of one part C group: the part `C`, the group key, a label, the drop list `CG[key][1]`, and the text for n.
- That text holds the number of pairs (the number of drops), the number of intervals, the number of processes with their tags, the sessions from `sess`, and the fixed words `1 boot`.
segments.heading: Section 3.4: the drops per part and the verdict for Q1

segments.text:
`q1p` lists the 9 rows of the Q1 table. Each entry holds the part, the group key, the label of the pair, a list of drops in percent, and the text for n.
- 5 entries for the groups of part C, built by `cpair`.
- Part L with `dl`, control I with `di`, and F72d12 with `df`. Each list holds the `drop_asmread` of every pair of that data set (lines 390 to 392).
- Part A with `dpa`: the 6 drops between the process medians (line 395).
- The numbers in the n texts are `len` of the drop list and counts from `gL`, `gA` and `gI`. `gL` and `gI` count asmread records, and `gA` counts `bw_new read` records. The words "per kernel", "1 boot", "no session" and "1 process" are fixed text.

**The smallest and the largest drop of each row.** For each entry the loop takes `min(ds)` and `max(ds)` of its drop list. No mean and no median of the drops is used.
- The table of the facts sheet shows both values with 1 decimal, rounded half up by `pc`.
- `V['q1_parts']` gets one entry per row. It holds both values rounded to 2 decimals by the Python function `round`. The label is stored without its backquotes.
- Example, part A: 28.5 % and 31.8 % in the facts sheet, 28.49 % and 31.78 % in facts.json [Ref4] [Ref6].
- The bullet after the table is fixed text: part C has one row per group.
